[Third-price auction, n=5, k=3. For i.i.d. uniform values, the symmetric Bayes–Nash equilibrium is linear: b(v) = (n-1)/(n-k+1) * v = 4/3 * v. With my private value v = 17, the equilibrium bid is 4/3 * 17 = 22.666..., so I round to the allowed $0.1 increment. This bid maximizes expected profit given others follow the equilibrium strategy.]

[With no prior rounds, I use a simple, robust strategy: bid my true value. In a third-price auction with five bidders, bidding truthfully is a reasonable, low-regret approach when others' strategies are unknown; it wins when my value is high relative to others and avoids systematic overbidding. Values are redrawn independently, so this approach maximizes expected long-run profit under symmetric uncertain opponents and keeps payment anchored by others' bids (third-highest). ]

I have a private value of $34 and face a 5‑bidder sealed‑bid auction where the winner pays the third‑highest bid. With independent private values and a single round, bidding my true value is a robust strategy: it lets me win exactly when post‑auction payoff (value − third‑highest) is likely positive, and avoids inducing a win that forces me to pay more than my value. I will therefore submit a bid equal to my value to maximize expected long‑run profit under uncertainty.

[This is a third-price sealed-bid with 5 bidders; if I win I pay the second-highest of the other four bids. My private value is high (45/49) and draws are independent with no history to learn from. Bidding my true value is a safe, aggressive strategy: it maximizes my chance to win when the item is valuable to me while the price paid is set by others' bids, not mine. Given no prior rounds and uniform values, I will bid my value to capture positive expected surplus when others are lower.]
